name: Interactive rebase
about: The rebase plan as a buffer, with the commit under the cursor beside it
_about: git opens an editor three times during a rebase: on the plan, on a
message it has been asked to reword, and — through the files it could
not merge — on the conflict. This does not replace any of that. It
makes textfold the editor git asks for, and makes those buffers worth
having opened.
textfold --install rebase
git config --global sequence.editor textfold
git config --global core.editor textfold
Then `git rebase -i` in a terminal opens the plan here, and so does
`rebase/start` in the palette. The two are the same rebase.
The plan is the file git wrote, in a buffer, so the cursor, selections,
`move-line-up`, undo and search all work on it already. What this adds
is the three things a buffer cannot know on its own:
* Alt-3 shows the commit under the cursor as a diff. Deciding between
squash and drop by looking at the change is the whole argument for
doing a rebase in an editor.
* The plan is checked on save and the answers go in the margin — a
squash on the first line, a sha that is not in the range, a plan
with nothing left to apply.
* Alt-2 says what git is actually doing: what is done, what stopped
it, which files are unmerged, and what is left.
`rebase/continue` is the whole gesture rather than the git command:
it refuses while a resolved file is unsaved or still has a conflict
marker in it, takes you to the line, stages what you resolved, and then
continues — with a reworded or squashed message opening in a buffer
instead of being taken silently.
How git is handed back to this window: this script in `--editor` mode
is what `$GIT_EDITOR` points at while a rebase runs. It connects to the
textfold that started it, asks for the file to be opened, and blocks
until the buffer is closed. Closing it exits zero, which is git's own
signal to carry on; calling the rebase off exits non-zero, which is
git's own signal to put everything back.
